strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP problem: measuring graded informational contribution in human–AI writing. The limitations appropriately distinguish this construct from creativity and legal authorship.
The proposed prompt-aware score is simple and transparent, measuring the reduction in output surprisal provided by the input without training a separate evaluator.

Experiments cover four domains, six generation models, two scoring models, repeated generations, and WildChat interactions. The broadly consistent ordering of polishing, summary-based generation, and sparse prompting provides useful evidence for coarse discrimination.

The 1,500-pair human study provides additional evidence, with three annotators and 91.47% unanimous agreement. Appendices document source datasets, generation prompts, model versions, and threshold selection.
weaknesses: The central percentage interpretation needs stronger justification. Equation 5 computes a pointwise log-likelihood ratio, rather than mutual information averaged over a joint distribution. The paper also does not establish that its unconditional language-model probability is the marginal corresponding to the prompt-conditioned distribution. Individual scores can be negative, so the shared-information diagram and proportional attribution interpretation do not follow directly from standard mutual-information properties. A conditional coding-cost reduction is a meaningful statistic, but its interpretation as a human contribution percentage remains insufficiently validated.

The output-only minimum-contribution claim exceeds the supporting derivation. Appendix B derives a lower bound conditional on a chosen plausibility threshold, then substitutes that bound as the minimum estimate in Equation 10 without demonstrating tightness or attainability by any prompt. Selecting the conditional-surprisal threshold as an empirical mean plus one standard deviation provides no guaranteed coverage for actual generations. Held-out coverage, approximation-error analysis, and sensitivity of the resulting percentages are needed.

The output-only estimator is exactly a monotonic transformation of ordinary model surprisal: writing H = I(y)/N and c = -log(tau), Equation 10 becomes 1 - c/H. For a fixed scoring model and threshold, it therefore produces identical rankings and ROC-AUC to average negative log likelihood or perplexity. The detection results in Table 2 cannot validate either the threshold calibration or the minimum-contribution interpretation. This equivalence should be explicit, with evidence addressing what the proposed interpretation adds.

The evaluation establishes coarse ordering more convincingly than general measurement validity. Human-evaluation pairs are selected only when the proposed score differs by more than 0.1; consequently, the reported 95.93% prompt-aware and 92.87% output-only agreement apply to this selected subset. Unfiltered and within-generation-mode comparisons are missing, as are input/output length and lexical or semantic overlap baselines that could explain the synthetic category separation. WildChat class differences and surrogate-model distribution plots likewise do not establish calibration of individual percentages.

Exact reproducibility remains limited despite the useful setup descriptions. The manuscript provides no code or constructed-data release location and leaves consequential likelihood-scoring conventions unclear, including unconditional context, chat templates, scored special tokens, and temperature rescaling. These details can materially change both scores and threshold values. Resolving these implementation gaps and the central attribution-validation concerns requires substantive revision before a sound Findings recommendation.
